newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Shell hopes for deal with Nigeria's Ogonis.
newsitem.headline: Shell hopes for deal with Nigeria's Ogonis.

text.p: Royal Dutch Shell hopes a deal to enable it to return to Nigeria's politically volatile Ogoniland may be possible this year.

Shell's manager for community and the environment in the eastern region said Shell was talking to various local groups -- including the Movement for the Survival of Ogoni People (MOSOP), once headed by hanged activist Ken Saro-Wiwa.
"The process of reconciliation is underway and before the end of the year there will be a breakthrough," Victor Dania told journalists in the eastern city of Port Harcourt on Thursday.

Driven from Ogoniland in 1993 by MOSOP sabotage of its installations, Shell came under fire from campaigners worldwide after the 1995 execution of Saro-Wiwa and eight fellow activists for the murder of pro-government chiefs.

They blamed Shell for not putting pressure on military ruler General Sani Abacha to spare the lives of the nine, who campaigned for rights for the half a million Ogonis and against environmental damage they say Shell caused.
Aware of damage to the company's global image, Shell has tried to mend fences with the Ogonis, but has so far been spurned by radicals.
"In terms of our image and community relations it will be nice to go back to Ogoniland and demonstrate that we do care," Dania said.
"The rift between the Ogonis themselves is perhaps deeper than with any outside body. There is MOSOP on the ground and MOSOP overseas, sometimes you wonder if their agenda is the same," he added.

Dania said Shell's plan for Ogoniland includes cleaning up oil spills and carrying out community development programmes, which he said had begun with the award of contracts to remove pollution and a programme to provide jobs for youths.
"Everything we are doing so far is towards reconciliation, not production. We have not gone back for production and I don't know when we are going back," Dania said.
After reconciliation it would take two to three years to resume production, allowing enough time to repair damaged installations and develop new reserves, he said.
When Shell pulled out, production in Ogoniland was only about 25,000 barrels per day from the company's total production in Nigeria of about one million barrels per day.

Rivalries, sometimes erupting in violence, abound between the many ethnic groups of Nigeria's oil-producing south and southeast -- one of the most densely populated regions of the West African country of over 100 million
